description: Read two articles, watch three videos, and suddenly you know how to fix the economy, the schools, and your brother-in-law. Most of us are a lot more sure than we are informed, and that gets loud around a Thanksgiving table.

In the final week of *Up Here*, Forrest Jenan climbs one last mountain, and it's one most of us have stood on a time or two: Mount Stupid. Forrest asks what happens when we climb back down and let Jesus teach us something brand new.
scripture: While he was still speaking, a bright cloud covered them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased. Listen to him!” When the disciples heard this, they fell facedown to the ground, terrified.
ideas: In 1847, some of the best doctors in Europe at Vienna General Hospital were unknowingly killing their patients.

Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that doctors moved from autopsies straight to the maternity ward without cleaning their hands. When he required a chlorinated lime wash, deaths dropped from about 12 percent to roughly 2 percent.
Many doctors resisted him, because accepting the evidence meant admitting they had been part of the problem.
The Dunning-Kruger effect says sometimes we don’t know enough to realize how little we know. Welcome to Mount Stupid.
Confirmation bias leads us to embrace information that confirms what we believe and dismiss information that challenges it.

ideas.text: says there is more hope for a fool than for someone who is wise in their own eyes.

ideas: The Greek word for disciple, mathētēs, means learner. You can’t be a disciple and think you know it all.
Peter had the right answer about Jesus and still misunderstood what it meant. On the Mount of Transfiguration, God interrupted him with, “Listen to him!”
Asking honest questions is a sign you’re finally willing to learn. In the Bible, the closer people get to God, the less impressed they are with themselves.
Certainty is never the destination… growth is. Three words worth practicing: “I was wrong.” Let’s climb down from Mount Stupid and let Jesus teach us something brand new.
questions: What’s something you were absolutely certain about when you were younger that you’ve completely changed your mind about?

questions.text: . Forrest said the problem isn’t that we don’t know something, it’s that we’re convinced we already do. Where do you see that in the world right now, and where might you see it in yourself?
. Peter gets the answer exactly right, and moments later he pulls Jesus aside to correct him. Where have you had the right answer and still missed what it meant?
. While Peter was still talking, God interrupted with, “Listen to him!” What tends to keep you from listening to Jesus: busyness, being sure you’re right, or something else?

questions: Asking honest questions is a sign you’re finally willing to learn. How has a question about faith helped you grow?
Moses, Isaiah, Job, and Peter all came away from meeting God with a bigger view of God and a more realistic view of themselves. How has getting closer to God changed the way you see yourself?
“I was wrong” … when was the last time you said those words? Who could you ask a question this week instead of correcting?

parts.text: What if we’re not nearly as different from those doctors as we’d like to think?
What if there are things we’re absolutely convinced about right now that we’re absolutely wrong about?
Our ability to recognize what we don't know.

They weren’t just wrong about the answers.

They were wrong about how wrong they were.
Sometimes we don’t know enough to realize how little we know.
When you’re standing on top of Mount Stupid, you don't think you're standing on Mount Stupid.
CONFIRMATION BIAS
Our tendency to embrace information that confirms what we already believe, while dismissing information that challenges it.

The problem isn’t simply that you don't know something.

The problem is that you’re convinced you already do.
“If God agrees with me and you disagree with me ... well, clearly you’re the problem.”
We can start confusing our confidence in God with our confidence in our own understanding of God.
You can’t be a disciple and think you know it all.

Peter wasn’t wrong about who Jesus was.

He was wrong about what it meant.
We become
so certain
about what God is supposed to be doing that we
struggle to recognize
what God is actually doing.
When was the last time you changed your mind about something important?

I don’t know.

I hadn’t thought about that.

I was wrong.
The
closer
we get to God, the
less impressed
we should be with ourselves.
You can know an awful lot about Jesus and still be really difficult to correct.
